title: Call Him by His names
hook: the beautiful names again, in their home verse (7:180)

segments.voice: Yesterday: mithaq, the covenant of Alast. Your line was we said yes. Did something feel like remembering? Today, the beautiful names come back, this time in the verse they call home. Day four hundred fourteen.

Back on day two hundred thirty-two, you started a list: the most beautiful names of Allah. The Merciful, the Forgiving, the Provider, the Patient. Maybe you've still got it on a phone note somewhere. Lists of names are lovely to read, and easy to treat like a museum: beautiful things behind glass. But the verse those names come from, in surah seven, doesn't hand them over to be admired. It hands them over to be used. It says what they're for in four words.
screen: `DAY 232, A LIST BEGUN.` → `NAMES BEHIND GLASS?` → `WHAT THEY'RE FOR.`

segments.voice: Verse one-eighty, in Pickthall's words: “Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them.” In Arabic: wa lillahi al-asma' al-husna, fad'uhu biha. To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them. The word for call, ud'u, is the same root as du'a. The names aren't only to know. They're to use, the way you use someone's name to get their attention. So scholars teach matching the name to the need. When you need provision, call on ar-Razzaq, the Provider. When you've done wrong, al-Ghafur, the Forgiving. When you're afraid, as-Salam, Peace. The verse goes on: leave those who distort His names. The verb is yulhiduna, from a root meaning to swerve to one side. A grave in much of the Muslim world has a lahd, a niche dug into the side wall: the same root. To distort the names is to bend them away from what they mean. How many names are there? A hadith in Bukhari says Allah has ninety-nine names, and whoever counts them will enter paradise; scholars explained count as learning them, understanding them, and living by them. But many scholars also held that ninety-nine is not the limit. They cite a du'a reported from the Prophet ﷺ that asks by every name Allah has named Himself, including those He kept hidden with Himself. The list you started is a door, not the whole house. The phrase al-asma' al-husna appears in four places in the Qur'an. This is where the command comes with it.
screen: `FAD'UHU BIHA — CALL ON HIM BY THEM.` · `MATCH THE NAME TO THE NEED.` · `ILHAD — TO SWERVE ASIDE.` · `NINETY-NINE, AND MORE.` · then, large: `THE NAMES ARE FOR CALLING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Name to yourself one thing you need today, plainly: patience with a child, money for rent, courage for a conversation, rest. Now pick the name that fits it: the Patient, the Provider, the Strong, Peace. If you pray, you can call on Him by that name, quietly, a few times with the breath. If you don't, simply sit with the name and the need side by side. The bell holds the time.
Call Him by His names. Surah seven, verse one-eighty: to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them. Today's word.
screen: `CALL HIM BY HIS NAMES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the names are for calling. Today, when a need comes up, reach for the one name that fits it. Day four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Muslims often begin a du'a with the divine name that fits the request, such as ya Razzaq for provision or ya Ghafur for forgiveness, and many learn the ninety-nine names by heart.

match.prompt: match the name to the need — tap the pairs.

lahd: a niche dug to one side; ilhad, swerving aside.

fork.setup: you're anxious about money this month. 7:180 says call on Him by His names. which name fits best?
fork.reveal: scholars teach matching the name to the need: ar-Razzaq for provision.

trapdoor: what you thought: God has ninety-nine names.
what it means: the names belong to Allah and are given to be called on, matched to the need.

what a scholar hears: al-asma' al-husna appears in 7:180, 17:110, 20:8 and 59:24; Ibn Mas'ud's reported du'a (Musnad Ahmad) asks by names 'kept in the unseen', so most scholars hold the names are more than ninety-nine.
